actions.body: Recent data [source-d9addfec171d4b5d] highlights a serial association where dependence on AI training tools leads to 'body signal outsourcing'—a reduced capacity for athletes to monitor their own internal physical states. This outsourcing correlates with training decision hesitation and lower self-efficacy. While AI increases the scientific rigor of training programs, it creates a dependency loop that may undermine the foundational skill of self-regulation [source-fae5034da1e04868]. These findings suggest that AI integration requires explicit attention to maintaining user autonomy rather than just optimizing performance metrics [source-d8e6a4e1139d42cd]. Summary: AI-driven training systems improve data-backed decisions but can cause athletes to rely too heavily on the machine, potentially damaging their ability to interpret their own bodies and make independent decisions.
actions.lede: New research suggests that reliance on AI training recommendations may paradoxically reduce an athlete's ability to self-regulate.
actions.reason: Synthesizing athlete reliance evidence into an accessible summary of AI-dependency risks.
actions.title: The Autonomy Trade-off: AI Dependency in Sports Training

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=longitudinal+impact+of+AI-driven+decision+support+systems+on+user+autonomy+and+self-regulation+skills&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1016/j.dss.2026.114720\", \"title\": [\"Corrigendum to ‘Designing AI-driven augmented living spaces with spatial augmented reality to support the autonomy of individuals with amnestic mild cognitive impairment’ [Decision support systems (2026) 114652]\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dss.2026.114720\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 10]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6928898\", \"title\": [\"AI-Driven Healthcare Visualization and Its Impact on Clinical Decision Support Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"AI-driven healthcare visualization is emerging as a critical advancement in modern medical informatics, significantly enhancing the capabilities of Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS). By transforming large-scale and complex clinical datasets into interpretable visual formats, such as imaging overlays, predictive dashboards, and interactive diagnostic charts, these systems improve the accuracy, speed, and reliability of clinical decision-making. Integrating machine learning and data visualization techniques, AI enables healthcare professionals to identify patterns, detect anomalies, and assess patient risks more effectively across diverse medical domains, including radiology, cardiology, and chronic disease management. Despite these advantages, challenges such as data privacy concerns, model interpretability limitations, algorithmic bias, and integration difficulties with existing healthcare infrastructure continue to hinder widespread adoption. This paper examines the role of AI-driven visualization in strengthening Clinical Decision Support Systems, highlighting its contributions to diagnostic improvement, workflow optimization, and patient care enhancement, while also addressing its ethical, technical, and operational constraints.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6928898\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1016/j.dss.2024.114193\", \"title\": [\"Navigating autonomy and control in human-AI delegation: User responses to technology- versus user-invoked task allocation\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dss.2024.114193\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2024, 5]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.21203/rs.3.rs-9362915/v1\", \"title\": [\"Trust in AI-Driven Decision Support Systems: Modeling the Dual Effects on User Innovation and Technostress\"], \"abstract\": \"Abstract\\n

When employees trust AI-driven decision support systems (AI-DSS), does that trust help or hurt them? This study argues it does both at the same time. Drawing on Cognitive Appraisal Theory, Social Exchange Theory, and Technology Threat Avoidance Theory, we propose that trust in AI-DSS operates as a double-edged sword: it can free employees to think more creatively and generate new ideas (the empowerment pathway), yet it can also make them overly reliant on AI recommendations, creating stress and anxiety when the system changes or fails (the dependency pathway). Which effect dominates depends on two boundary conditions: employees with higher AI Literacy gain more from trust (innovation benefits), while stronger Organizational AI Support reduces the stress costs of dependency for everyone. We tested this model with a two-wave survey of 452 knowledge workers who use AI-DSS regularly. Results confirm both pathways: trust in AI-DSS significantly boosts user innovation behavior through perceived empowerment (indirect effect = 0.249), while simultaneously increasing technostress through perceived dependency (indirect effect = 0.175). AI Literacy amplifies the innovation benefit only above a critical threshold (scale score = 2.81), meaning that about one in four employees currently receives no innovation benefit from their trust. Organizational support, by contrast, reduces stress costs unconditionally, regardless of support level. A non-linear analysis further reveals an optimal trust zone: moderate-to-high trust maximizes net benefit, whereas excessive trust accelerates stress costs faster than it grows innovation returns. To estimate these effects robustly from Likert-scale survey data, we develop a Neural-Augmented Bayesian SEM (NB-SEM) framework that reduces estimation error by up to 51% compared with standard structural equation modeling. These findings suggest that the goal of AI-DSS governance should shift from simply building more trust to cultivating the right level of trust, supported by targeted AI literacy training and proactive organizational support structures.
